ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethics: The secondary data in the manuscript is exempt from IRB approval.

The validation studies have IRB approval (Validation of Confident Language: 22-09-26; Validation of Information Quality at the Post level: HUM00239109) Data Disclosures Preregistration: No pre-registration was obtained for the analyses of the secondary data.
We aimed to recruit 200 participants, and a total of 198 participants provided complete data.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> We aimed to recruit 200 participants, and a total of 198 participants provided complete data.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The preregistered primary analysis calculated the correlation between Certainty Lexicon scores and average human certainty ratings across the 90 posts. We also preregistered that the validation would be considered successful if this correlation was positive and statistically significant (two-sided p < .05). With 90 posts, the study had 80% power to detect a correlation of approximately r = .29 or larger.

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/qwen3-8-27b-fp8' to check the contents of 2 paragraphs that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. Some essential information could not be detected: software ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(power_type = "apriori", statistical_test = "correlation", sample_size = 90, alpha_level = 0.05, power = 0.8, effect_size = 0.29, effect_size_metric = "other", software = NA_character_), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "The preregistered primary analysis calculated the correlation between Certainty Lexicon scores and average human certainty ratings across the 90 posts. We also preregistered that the validation would be considered successful if this correlation was positive and statistically significant (two-sided p < .05). With 90 posts, the study had 80% power to detect a correlation of approximately r = .29 or larger."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 17 columns across 2 data files.
#### Issues Identified

2 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("test.csv", "train.csv"), Column = c("comment_text", "comment_text"), Issues = c("🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 167 characters, 100% distinct) may contain...", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Values look like personal information: ip_address (15 values, 5%); Free-text column (median 218 characters, 100% distinct) may contain..." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 2 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Misinformation on online platforms is of great concern for democracy, public health, and civic discourse.
In fast-paced feeds, users often rely on heuristics when deciding what to attend to, believe, and share.
One such heuristic is confidence, which, prior research shows, is treated as a cue of knowledge and credibility.

Yet, we show that in over 4 million posts across seven social media platforms and one messaging app, confidence is negatively associated with information quality: posts written with greater confidence are more likely to link to lower-quality news domains and to contain false claims -even controlling for user baselines, toxicity, political lean, emotionality, and valence.
Furthermore, we find that confident posts receive more engagement.

Together, these results reveal a problematic asymmetry in online information environments: a widespread linguistic cue that is likely to be read as a signal of knowledge, and to attract engagement, is in fact associated with lower-quality information.

The spread of misinformation on social media (1) has become one of the more salient concerns in the context of the functioning of democratic societies, the integrity of public health communication, and the epistemic foundations of civic discourse.
It is not just what is reported but how it is written-and framed-that determines public uptake and belief (2).

text.text: In fast-paced online environments, users are frequently exposed to news headlines, social commentary, and linked articles in rapid succession.
Under such conditions, prior work suggests that users often rely on surface-level cues rather than deliberative processing to assess content credibility (3) (4) (5).
text.formatted: Under such conditions, prior work suggests that users often rely on surface-level cues rather than deliberative processing to assess content credibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: These heuristics-including linguistic shortcuts that affect judgment-can be consequential.
Indeed, growing evidence suggests that the stylistic features of how information is conveyed may be quite influential (6).
text.formatted: Indeed, growing evidence suggests that the stylistic features of how information is conveyed may be quite influential <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref>.

text.text: One important cue that has not been studied in misinformation contexts is confidence.
When communicators convey a strong sense of conviction through their language, audiences infer greater credibility, expertise, and status, and become more receptive to their claims.

Experiments indicate that people apply a confidence heuristic: more confident communicators are judged as more knowledgeable and their arguments more persuasive, even when objective knowledge is held constant (7).
text.formatted: Experiments indicate that people apply a confidence heuristic: more confident communicators are judged as more knowledgeable and their arguments more persuasive, even when objective knowledge is held constant <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: Laboratory and field evidence shows that confident wording increases perceived credibility and engagement (8, 9), while expressed confidence elevates perceived expertise/status, which in turn boosts influence and persuasive power (10).
text.formatted: Laboratory and field evidence shows that confident wording increases perceived credibility and engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9)</ref>, while expressed confidence elevates perceived expertise/status, which in turn boosts influence and persuasive power <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref>.

text.text: Confidence is therefore a cue that proxies for knowledge and competence.
This makes it particularly relevant in information environments where the central question is whether a source is credible.
However, expressed confidence may not necessarily reflect genuine knowledge or conviction.
For example, people use confident language to get attention, regardless of whether their claims are accurate (11).
text.formatted: For example, people use confident language to get attention, regardless of whether their claims are accurate <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref>.

text.text: Further, when people feel doubtful, they often respond by advocating for their beliefs more forcefully by using strong, unequivocal language (12).
text.formatted: Further, when people feel doubtful, they often respond by advocating for their beliefs more forcefully by using strong, unequivocal language <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, confident expression may actually mark uncertainty rather than knowledge.

This raises an ironic possibility for social media and misinformation: the very language that people use as a sign of knowledge may systematically signal lower knowledge and lower-quality, misinformative content (vs. higher-quality content).
Moreover, confidently worded news posts might also attract greater engagement (8).
text.formatted: Moreover, confidently worded news posts might also attract greater engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>.

text.text: If so, a cue people rely on to signal knowledge would instead amplify the information that deserves the least attention.
Despite this, to our knowledge, prior work has yet to examine whether expressed confidence is systematically associated with information quality.
Therefore, in the present work we shed light on this question empirically.
Specifically, we ask whether confident wording -the degree of conviction or certainty expressed through language -is associated with information quality.

Using a dataset of over 4 million social-media posts linking to independently-rated news domains, we measure confidence using a validated linguistic measure (13) and news quality using a wisdom-of-experts rating aggregated across professional fact-checkers, journalists, and academics (14) as well as direct fact-checking using AI.
text.formatted: Using a dataset of over 4 million social-media posts linking to independently-rated news domains, we measure confidence using a validated linguistic measure <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref> and news quality using a wisdom-of-experts rating aggregated across professional fact-checkers, journalists, and academics <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref> as well as direct fact-checking using AI.

text.text: Our models adjust for baseline writing style across users via user fixed effects.
This allows us to compare higher-versus lower-confidence posts from the same user, accounting for individual differences in writing style and source-selection tendencies.
We also account for political lean because both news quality and the use of confident language may vary systematically with the ideological orientation of the sources being shared.
Beyond that, we control for a range of linguistic factors that could otherwise contribute to the association between confidence, quality, and engagement.

Specifically, prior research finds toxicity to be associated with lower-quality information and higher engagement (15, 16), emotionality and valence to predict content virality and diffusion (17) (18) (19), including differences in the spread of true versus false information (20) as well as to help distinguish fake from real news (21), and post length to be associated with both information quality (22) and greater engagement on social media (23).
text.formatted: Specifically, prior research finds toxicity to be associated with lower-quality information and higher engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16)</ref>, emotionality and valence to predict content virality and diffusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref>, including differences in the spread of true versus false information <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(20)</ref> as well as to help distinguish fake from real news <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(21)</ref>, and post length to be associated with both information quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref> and greater engagement on social media <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(23)</ref>.

text.text: This allows us to test whether confidence has an association with information quality and engagement over and above these related linguistic and content features.
We additionally examine whether confident news posts also attract more engagement (diffusion).

Prior work has established that confident language increases engagement in commercial and social contexts (8), and we test whether this pattern extends to news, and whether it replicates at scale across a diverse set of platforms.
text.formatted: Prior work has established that confident language increases engagement in commercial and social contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>, and we test whether this pattern extends to news, and whether it replicates at scale across a diverse set of platforms.

text.text: Our core finding is that linguistic confidence is robustly and negatively associated with information quality.

This association emerges across eight platforms, in both news headlines and user-generated language, across topical domains and over time, and after accounting for a range of linguistic and content factors.
Moreover, when information quality is assessed directly at the level of individual posts, more confident language is associated with a greater likelihood of false or misleading claims.
Confidence-a cue people often use as a signal of knowledge-is therefore, on average, associated with lower-quality and misleading information.

Our data consist of 4,309,213 primary posts (excluding reshares and replies) containing links to one of 8,798 news domains, collected from X, LinkedIn, Gab, GETTR, Truth Social, Mastodon, Bluesky, and Telegram, primarily during January 2024 (see Methods for collection details and platform-specific exceptions).
Each post is characterized by three main variables.

News quality is the rating of the linked domain from a "wisdom of experts" aggregation of fact-checker, journalist, and academic assessments (14), normalized to a 0-1 scale on which higher values indicate higher-quality sources.
text.formatted: News quality is the rating of the linked domain from a "wisdom of experts" aggregation of fact-checker, journalist, and academic assessments <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref>, normalized to a 0-1 scale on which higher values indicate higher-quality sources.

text.text: Linguistic confidence is the score assigned to the post text by the Certainty Lexicon (13), ranging from 0 ("very uncertain") to 9 ("very certain"); we validated this measure against human judgments on a sample of our posts (SI).
Political lean is the lean of the linked domain, rated from -5 (strongly left) to 5 (strongly right).
In additional models we also control for language toxicity (percentile-transformed), emotionality and valence , and word count.
We imputed missing values for control variables with mean value.
We began by analyzing the association between news quality and linguistic confidence across different platforms.
To do so, we predict the quality of the news domain linked in each post (higher values indicate higher-quality sources) using the linguistic confidence of the post as the main predictor.
We also include the political lean of the news source (higher values indicate more conservative) as a control variable.
The primary analysis is an ordinary least squares regression predicting domain level quality using linguistic confidence.
Differences across platforms are handled by estimating separate models for each platform.
Standard errors are clustered on user to account for repeated observations from the same (in robustness analyses, we also user fixed effects).

All variables are z-scored within the platform before estimation, so each coefficient represents the change in news quality, in standard deviations, associated with a one-standard-deviation increase in linguistic confidence within that platform.

Following Mosleh et al., (2025), The platform-level coefficients and their standard errors are then combined in a random-effects meta-analysis (REML estimation, inverse-variance weighting) to obtain the overall estimate, its 95% confidence interval, and a test of heterogeneity across platforms.

This approach allows every model parameter to be estimated separately for each platform, rather than constrained to be equal as in a single pooled model (which is important as platforms differ markedly in user populations, posting norms, affordances, moderation, and the distribution of news quality and political lean), while still yielding an overall estimate and an assessment of heterogeneity across platforms in the key estimand.

As hypothesized, across all platforms, we find that posts written with greater confidence link to lower quality news domains (b=-0.037, SE=0.009, z=-4.31, p<0.001 without controlling for political lean; b=-0.024, SE=0.005, z=-5.29, p<0.001 with controlling for political lean; Figure 1A).
text.formatted: As hypothesized, across all platforms, we find that posts written with greater confidence link to lower quality news domains (b=-0.037, SE=0.009, z=-4.31, p<0.001 without controlling for political lean; b=-0.024, SE=0.005, z=-5.29, p<0.001 with controlling for political lean; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>).

text.text: Because within-platform standardization could in principle compress differences between platforms, we re-estimated the same models on the unstandardized variables, so that the coefficient represents the change in news quality (on its 0-1 scale) per one-point increase in linguistic confidence (on its 0-9 scale).

The results are qualitatively the same (b=-0.008, SE=0.002, z=-3.83, p<0.001 without controlling for political lean; b=-0.005, SE=0.001, z=-4.38, p<0.001 with controlling for political lean; Figure SI3c).
text.formatted: The results are qualitatively the same (b=-0.008, SE=0.002, z=-3.83, p<0.001 without controlling for political lean; b=-0.005, SE=0.001, z=-4.38, p<0.001 with controlling for political lean; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">SI3c</ref>).

text.text: The association is negative on every platform, though its magnitude varies.

A random-effects meta-analysis indicates significant between-platform heterogeneity (Q(7) = 43.72, I² = 90.14%, τ² = 0.0005 without controlling for political lean and with standardizing within each platform).

Much of this variation reflects differences in the political composition of the news shared on each platform: adjusting for political lean reduces the estimated between-platform variance by roughly 80% (τ² = 0.0005 without control versus 0.0001 with control).

Consistent with this, political lean is positively associated with linguistic confidence (b = 0.027, SE = 0.002, t = 15.82, p < .001) and negatively associated with news quality (b = -0.419, SE = 0.009, t = -48.77, p < .001), even after accounting for other controls (Table SI3).
text.formatted: Consistent with this, political lean is positively associated with linguistic confidence (b = 0.027, SE = 0.002, t = 15.82, p < .001) and negatively associated with news quality (b = -0.419, SE = 0.009, t = -48.77, p < .001), even after accounting for other controls (Table <ref type="table">SI3</ref>).

text.text: Importantly, however, the negative association between linguistic confidence and news quality persists after adjusting for political lean, suggesting that the relationship is not simply an outcome of differences in the political orientation of the news being shared.
Next, as a complement to the meta-analytic approach, we pooled posts from all platforms into a single regression.
Variables are z-scored on the pooled sample and standard errors are clustered by user.

We found a similar significant negative relationship between news domain quality and the linguistic confidence of post (b = -0.054, SE = 0.003, t = -19.66, p < 0.001 without controls; b = -0.028, SE = 0.002, t = -14.41, p < 0.001 controlling for political lean; b = -0.030, SE = 0.002, t = -16.23, p < 0.001 controlling for political lean, emotionality, valence, language toxicity, and number of words).
text.formatted: We found a similar significant negative relationship between news domain quality and the linguistic confidence of post (b = -0.054, SE = 0.003, t = -19.66, p < 0.001 without controls; b = -0.028, SE = 0.002, t = -14.41, p < 0.001 controlling for political lean; b = -0.030, SE = 0.002, t = -16.23, p < 0.001 controlling for political lean, emotionality, valence, language toxicity, and number of words).

text.text: Adding platform fixed effects, so that the relationship is identified from within-platform variation only, leaves the pattern intact (b = -0.028, SE = 0.002, t = -15.45, p < 0.001 without controls; b = -0.018, SE = 0.002, t = -11.69, p < 0.001 controlling for political lean; b = -0.019, SE = 0.001, t = -13.24, p < 0.001 controlling for political lean, emotionality, valence, language toxicity, and number of words).
text.formatted: Adding platform fixed effects, so that the relationship is identified from within-platform variation only, leaves the pattern intact (b = -0.028, SE = 0.002, t = -15.45, p < 0.001 without controls; b = -0.018, SE = 0.002, t = -11.69, p < 0.001 controlling for political lean; b = -0.019, SE = 0.001, t = -13.24, p < 0.001 controlling for political lean, emotionality, valence, language toxicity, and number of words).

text.text: Additionally, in the analysis pooling posts from all platforms into a single regression, we account for variation in user-level baseline in addition to platform-level baseline in the usage of confident language by including user fixed effects.

This model also shows a similar pattern (b = -0.007, SE = 0.001, t = -7.53, p < 0.001 without controls; b = -0.005, SE = 0.001, t = -6.22, p < 0.001 when controlling for political lean; b = -0.005, SE = 0.001, t = -6.12 with all controls; See Figure SI3a-c for individual platforms).
text.formatted: This model also shows a similar pattern (b = -0.007, SE = 0.001, t = -7.53, p < 0.001 without controls; b = -0.005, SE = 0.001, t = -6.22, p < 0.001 when controlling for political lean; b = -0.005, SE = 0.001, t = -6.12 with all controls; See Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">SI3a-c</ref> for individual platforms).

text.text: Across all analytic approaches -cross-platform meta-analysis, pooled regression, and controls for political lean and other linguistic featuresthe relationship between linguistic confidence and lower news quality is consistent and robust.

Crucially, this relationship holds even within users: the same individual, when posting with greater confidence, links to lower-quality news -ruling out the possibility that the pattern reflects robust between-user differences in baseline writing style or systematic preferences for particular news sources.

The Certainty Lexicon scores only the 4 million posts containing at least one confidence dictionary term that make up our primary sample; posts with news links that do not contain any confidence dictionary terms (typically short posts) are excluded from the main analyses by listwise deletion.

To check that this exclusion does not drive our results, we re-estimated the pooled platform-fixed-effects models on all posts, assigning unscored posts the scale midpoint and adding a missing-score indicator (which absorbs the mean difference between scored and unscored posts, so the confidence slope does not depend on the fill-in value).

The association between confidence and news quality was essentially unchanged: (without controls) b = -0.028, SE = 0.002, t=-15.45, p<0.001 with listwise deletion versus b = -0.023, SE = 0.001, t=-16.36 , p<0.001 with all posts retained; (with controls) b = -0.019, SE = 0.001, t=-13.25, p<0.001 versus b = -0.016, SE = 0.001, t=-13.3, p<0.001.
text.formatted: The association between confidence and news quality was essentially unchanged: (without controls) b = -0.028, SE = 0.002, t=-15.45, p<0.001 with listwise deletion versus b = -0.023, SE = 0.001, t=-16.36 , p<0.001 with all posts retained; (with controls) b = -0.019, SE = 0.001, t=-13.25, p<0.001 versus b = -0.016, SE = 0.001, t=-13.3, p<0.001.

text.text: Posts without confidence scores link to domains have similar average quality to posts with confidence scores (0.691 vs 0.684), indicating that omitted posts do not differ systematically in the quality of news they share.
While widely used in prior work (26) (27) (28) (29), domain-level quality scores assign the same rating to all content originating from the same website.
text.formatted: While widely used in prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(26)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(27)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(29)</ref>, domain-level quality scores assign the same rating to all content originating from the same website.

text.text: To assess the robustness of our results using a more granular, post-level measure, we annotated all posts using Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite (see SI for prompt).

We also validated the scoring by Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, replicating prior results (30), whereby Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite agrees with professional fact-checkers as much or more than professional fact-checkers agree with each other (see SI for details).

We conducted a logistic regression predicting whether the post includes misleading or false claims (coded 1 if the LLM rated the central claim False or Misleading, 0 if otherwise), with linguistic confidence z-scored and standard errors clustered by user, so odds ratios represent the change in the odds of a false or misleading claim per one-standard-deviation increase in confidence.

Consistent with our analysis of domain-level quality rating, we find a significant relationship between linguistic confidence and post-level accuracy ratings: posts written with more confident language were more likely to contain false or misleading information (OR = 1.10, SE = 0.005, z=21.4, p<0.001 without controls and without user fixed-effect; OR=1.05, SE=0.003, z=18.4, p<0.001 without controls and with user fixed-effect; OR = 1.10, SE = 0.004, z = 24.9, p<0.001 with controls for political lean, emotionality, valence, language toxicity, and number of word and without user fixed-effect; and OR = 1.06, SE = 0.003, z = 21.0, p<0.001 with user fixed-effect and with controls).
text.formatted: Consistent with our analysis of domain-level quality rating, we find a significant relationship between linguistic confidence and post-level accuracy ratings: posts written with more confident language were more likely to contain false or misleading information (OR = 1.10, SE = 0.005, z=21.4, p<0.001 without controls and without user fixed-effect; OR=1.05, SE=0.003, z=18.4, p<0.001 without controls and with user fixed-effect; OR = 1.10, SE = 0.004, z = 24.9, p<0.001 with controls for political lean, emotionality, valence, language toxicity, and number of word and without user fixed-effect; and OR = 1.06, SE = 0.003, z = 21.0, p<0.001 with user fixed-effect and with controls).

text.text: This confirms that the confidence-quality relationship reflects the actual informational content of individual posts, not merely the aggregate reputational score of the outlets they link to.
We further assess the relationship between the average linguistic confidence and the average quality of news shared across each of the eight platforms.

When averaging these characteristics at the platform level (Figure 2), we observe a strong negative correlation: platforms with posts containing higher average linguistic confidence tend to also have posts containing links to lower-quality news sources (Pearson r across the eight platform means, n = 8; r=-0.877, p =.004).
text.formatted: When averaging these characteristics at the platform level (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>), we observe a strong negative correlation: platforms with posts containing higher average linguistic confidence tend to also have posts containing links to lower-quality news sources (Pearson r across the eight platform means, n = 8; r=-0.877, p =.004).

text.text: Additionally, we find a strong association between use of confident language and conservative political lean at the platform level (r=.913, p=0.002), justifying our use of political lean as a control.

Although all observations are from social-media posts, the textual source varies: some posts contain user-generated commentary attached to a news link, whereas others display only the headline text supplied by the news domain.

These texts are produced under different norms-idiosyncratic social expression versus professionally edited headline copy-so the confidence-quality association documented in aggregate could differ across them (cf.

To assess generalizability, we next examine whether the confidence-quality relationship holds across different textual sources, and whether it extends beyond outlet-level strategy to users' own expressive behavior, by focusing on a subset of N=41,040 unique headlines for which we extracted just the news headline (see Methods).
We use linear regression to predict news domain information quality from linguistic confidence of news headlines with cluster standard errors on news domain.

Consistent with our findings above, we find headlines written with greater linguistic confidence come from lower-quality domains (b = -0.103, SE = 0.026, t = -3.92, p < 0.001 without controls; b = -0.060, SE = 0.012, t = -5.17, p < 0.001 when controlling for political lean, emotionality, toxicity, valence, and number of words) (Fig 1C).
text.formatted: Consistent with our findings above, we find headlines written with greater linguistic confidence come from lower-quality domains (b = -0.103, SE = 0.026, t = -3.92, p < 0.001 without controls; b = -0.060, SE = 0.012, t = -5.17, p < 0.001 when controlling for political lean, emotionality, toxicity, valence, and number of words) (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1C</ref>).

text.text: Furthermore, we examine whether the relationship between confidence and content quality is confined to headline text-where it could be interpreted as a deliberate attention-grabbing tactic by low-quality news outlets-or whether it also extends to user-generated content.

To do so, for posts where we also obtained the headline text, we calculated the cosine similarity between the post text and the headline text (we did so to account for the platform affordances i.e., the post text and headline text may not exactly match due to variance from extra characters).

We find a significant relationship between confidence and content quality for cases where the post content and headline are not similar, suggesting that this relationship extends to user generated content as well (b = -0.040, SE = 0.002, t = -19.6, p < 0.001 where post and headline text cosine similarity <.9; b = -0.007, SE = 0.001, t = -7.27, p < 0.001 where post and headline text cosine similarity <.9 with user fixed-effect; b = -0.028 SE = 0.002, t = -11.4, p < 0.001 where post and headline text cosine similarity <.5; b = -0.005 SE = 0.001, t = -4.15, p < 0.001 where post and headline text cosine similarity <.5 with user fixed-effects; pooled OLS with platform fixed effects, user-clustered standard errors, on the subset of posts meeting each threshold).
text.formatted: We find a significant relationship between confidence and content quality for cases where the post content and headline are not similar, suggesting that this relationship extends to user generated content as well (b = -0.040, SE = 0.002, t = -19.6, p < 0.001 where post and headline text cosine similarity <.9; b = -0.007, SE = 0.001, t = -7.27, p < 0.001 where post and headline text cosine similarity <.9 with user fixed-effect; b = -0.028 SE = 0.002, t = -11.4, p < 0.001 where post and headline text cosine similarity <.5; b = -0.005 SE = 0.001, t = -4.15, p < 0.001 where post and headline text cosine similarity <.5 with user fixed-effects; pooled OLS with platform fixed effects, user-clustered standard errors, on the subset of posts meeting each threshold).

text.text: So, we find that the confidence-quality relation is predicted by linguistic confidence and is not simply an outcome of low-quality news outlets using confidence as a strategy to gain attention.
When we look at user generated content in the posts, the same negative association holds.

These results confirm that the confidence-quality relationship reflects two routes: not only the choices of low-quality news outlets, but also the spontaneous linguistic behavior of users amplifying that content.
We next examined whether the relationship between linguistic confidence and information quality holds across the political spectrum.

Whereas our primary analyses control for political lean, here we stratified posts into left-leaning (lean = -5 to -2), center (lean = -1 to 1), and right-leaning (lean = 2 to 5) groups based on the political lean of the shared news domain.

We estimated a single linear regression predicting information quality from linguistic confidence interacted with group indicators, controlling for platform (i.e., using platform fixed effects), with standard errors clustered by user.

Confidence was negatively associated with information quality within all three groups, both when controlling only for platform (left: b = -0.010, SE = 0.002, t = -5.92, p < .001; center: b = -0.010, SE = 0.002, t = -6.14, p < .001; right: b = -0.040, SE = 0.004, t = -9.14, p < .001) and when additionally controlling for toxicity, valence, emotionality, and post length (left: b = -0.010, SE = 0.002 , t = -6.1, p < .001; center: b = -0.009, SE = 0.002, t = -6.1, p < .001; right: b = -0.04, SE = 0.004, t = -9.25, p < .001; Fig. SI6; Fig SI7).
text.formatted: Confidence was negatively associated with information quality within all three groups, both when controlling only for platform (left: b = -0.010, SE = 0.002, t = -5.92, p < .001; center: b = -0.010, SE = 0.002, t = -6.14, p < .001; right: b = -0.040, SE = 0.004, t = -9.14, p < .001) and when additionally controlling for toxicity, valence, emotionality, and post length (left: b = -0.010, SE = 0.002 , t = -6.1, p < .001; center: b = -0.009, SE = 0.002, t = -6.1, p < .001; right: b = -0.04, SE = 0.004, t = -9.25, p < .001; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_9">SI6</ref>; Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">SI7</ref>).

text.text: Pairwise comparisons of the group-specific slopes showed no difference between the left-leaning and center groups (platform control only: Δb = 0.000, SE = 0.002, t = -0.20, p = .844; full controls: Δb = -0.001, SE = 0.002, t = -0.30, p = 0.766).

The negative association was, however, significantly stronger for right-leaning posts than for left-leaning posts (platform control only: Δb = -0.030, SE = 0.005, t = -6.38, p < .001; full controls: Δb = -0.030, SE = 0.005, t = -6.43, p < .001) or center posts (platform only: Δb = -0.031, SE = 0.005, t = -6.61, p < .001; full controls: Δb = -0.031, SE = 0.005, t = -6.71, p < .001).
text.formatted: The negative association was, however, significantly stronger for right-leaning posts than for left-leaning posts (platform control only: Δb = -0.030, SE = 0.005, t = -6.38, p < .001; full controls: Δb = -0.030, SE = 0.005, t = -6.43, p < .001) or center posts (platform only: Δb = -0.031, SE = 0.005, t = -6.61, p < .001; full controls: Δb = -0.031, SE = 0.005, t = -6.71, p < .001).

text.text: In sum, the negative confidence-quality association holds across the political spectrum, but is strongest among right-leaning content, indicating the strength of the association varies across the political spectrum, but political lean does not explain the main result.
We further examined whether the negative association between linguistic confidence and information quality was consistent across time and topics.

The association was robustly negative across the study period and remained significantly negative after accounting for day and platform fixed effects, both with and without additional linguistic controls (Fig. SI8).
text.formatted: The association was robustly negative across the study period and remained significantly negative after accounting for day and platform fixed effects, both with and without additional linguistic controls (Fig. <ref type="figure">SI8</ref>).

text.text: Similarly, the association was significantly negative across all four topical domains examined (politics, economy, health, and science), as well as posts outside these categories, both with and without controls (Fig. SI9).
text.formatted: Similarly, the association was significantly negative across all four topical domains examined (politics, economy, health, and science), as well as posts outside these categories, both with and without controls (Fig. <ref type="figure">SI9</ref>).

text.text: Full methodological details and results are reported in the SI.
Together, these findings provide further evidence of the robustness of the negative confidence-quality relationship across time and topical domains.

Having established a robust negative association between confidence and information quality, we next examine whether confident posts also attract greater engagement -the number of likes and reshares (diffusion).

To do this, we meta-analyze the results of separate linear regressions estimated for each platform, predicting engagement with posts (engagement counts are log-transformed to correct for skewness-log₁₀(likes + reshares + 1), likes only on Telegram -and variables are z-scored within platform).

Following (24), each model includes user fixed effects because of obvious user-level confounds when predicting engagement, such as number of followers, user position in the network, level of engagement of their followers, posting frequency, etc.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref>, each model includes user fixed effects because of obvious user-level confounds when predicting engagement, such as number of followers, user position in the network, level of engagement of their followers, posting frequency, etc.

text.text: In other words, we test whether the same user tends to receive more engagement when posting with higher versus lower linguistic confidence.
Consequently, any observed relationships cannot be attributed to differences in users or in their audiences.

The pattern of results suggests that overall a given user's posts with higher linguistic confidence receive significantly more engagement than their posts with lower linguistic confidence (b=0.011, SE=0.002, z=4.28, p<0.001 without controlling for political lean; b=0.011, SE=0.003, z=4.17, p<0.001; Figure 3A).

text.text: This paper examines how confidence operates within online information sharing environments and documents a systematic and consequential pattern in real-world platform discourse.

Across seven social media platforms and one messaging app -differing in content types, recommendation algorithms, content moderation policies, and user populations -and over 4 million posts, we find that linguistic confidence is robustly and negatively associated with news quality.
This relationship holds even after accounting for user baselines, political lean, toxicity, emotionality, and other linguistic features.

Importantly, this pattern also emerges when information quality is assessed at the level of individual posts: posts expressed with greater linguistic confidence are more likely to contain false or misleading claims as well.
The pattern is also evident at the platform level, such that platforms characterized by greater average linguistic confidence are those in which users share lower-quality news on average.

The core implication is that confidence -a cue people are most naturally inclined to treat as a marker of knowledge and credibility -is, on average, associated with lower-quality rather than higher-quality content online.
Compounding this, we also find that confident posts receive more engagement, extending prior work to the domain of news.
This suggests that platform dynamics reward a cue that, on average, points in the wrong direction about informational value.
Two additional findings hone the contribution.

First, the confidence-quality relationship holds after controlling for other linguistic dimensions that prior work has linked to engagement and information sharing, like emotionality, valence, word count, and toxicity.
This establishes that confidence is not simply a proxy for these other features.
Second, the relationship is not merely a result of low-quality news outlets writing confident headlines as an attention-grabbing strategy.

When we isolate user-generated content, the same negative association holds as when we examine headlines, suggesting that users' own expressive confidence plays an independent role in coupling confident language with low-quality information.

Together, these results indicate that the confidence-quality mismatch operates through at least two routes: the editorial choices of low-quality outlets, and the spontaneous linguistic behavior of the users who amplify their content.
The relationship also exhibits substantial generality.

The negative association between linguistic confidence and news quality was consistently observed across political leanings (although, it was stronger for right-leaning news sources), throughout the study period (rather than being concentrated around particular days), and emerged across science, politics, health, and economic news topics.
Thus, the confidence-quality relationship appears to characterize a general feature of news on social media rather than one tied to a political lean, a particular topical domain or moment in time.
Substantively, the results help reconcile how confident language is more likely to "win the feed" despite the lower quality of information conveyed.
Those pathways are desirable from the standpoint of persuasion and attention, but they also decouple confidence from actual quality of information.

In modern social media feeds, confidence is not simply a marker of persuasive skill; it is more likely to accompany lower-quality information that is nonetheless rewarded by engagement-sensitive ranking systems.
This reframing shifts the conversation from whether confidence persuades (it does) to what confidence is associated with in terms of content quality (in these data, lower quality on average).
We show that confident language-which has been shown to be more persuasivepersuades-is systematically associated with lower-quality news sources and with higher engagement.

By examining the association with quality separately from the association with engagement, our results clarify why confident, low-quality content is more likely to spreads: the same confidence cue that signals authority to readers is, on average, associated with lower informational value, and engagement-sensitive systems reward it.

Theoretical accounts of misinformation therefore need to incorporate confidence not merely as a driver of persuasion, but as a cue whose perceived meaning and empirical correlates diverge in information ecosystems.
Practically, the findings point beyond generic tone moderation.
If confidence is negatively associated with quality at scale, then interventions should focus on quality-aware ranking, transparency of source credibility, and context at the point of sharing.
In sum, our findings position confidence as a distinct construct in the psychology of misinformation-one that is persuasively potent yet negatively associated with information quality at scale.

By examining quality and engagement separately, we show that the same cue is associated both with greater engagement and with lower informational value, offering a principled constraint for theories of persuasion and social transmission.

We hope this decoupling framework invites work that builds theory forward-linking confidence to belief revision, memory, and networked influence-so models of communication account not only for whether messages persuade, but how their style relates to truth.

We leveraged a dataset of social media posts containing links to news domains shared on seven social media platforms and one messaging app (24): X (Twitter), LinkedIn, Gab, GETTR, Truth Social, Mastodon, Bluesky, and Telegram.
For X, by far the largest platform, we analyzed posts from 1 January to 31 January 2024.
For the seven smaller platforms we included all posts available at the time of data collection regardless of posting date, to maximize statistical power.
Our results are qualitatively unchanged when every platform is restricted to January 2024 (Figure SI3b) .
text.formatted: Our results are qualitatively unchanged when every platform is restricted to January 2024 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">SI3b</ref>) .

text.text: To ensure comparability across platforms, the selection of posts focused on those that (i) permit collection of individual-level posting data and (ii) allow users to share external links, which serve as our indicators of high-and low-quality content.

These criteria enabled consistent operationalization across platforms but excluded major image-and video-based sites such as YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram and also Facebook, where individual-level posting data are unavailable.

For X, LinkedIn, Gab, GETTR, and Truth Social, the platform's advanced search function was used to retrieve all posts containing links to any of 8,798 news domains for which we have quality ratings from Lin et al (2023) (see below), along with engagement metrics.

For Mastodon, the list of all available instances from https://instances.social/ was used and data collection was done on instances where data was publicly accessible, had at least 1,000 users, and contained posts including links to a rated news domain.
text.formatted: For Mastodon, the list of all available instances from <ref type="url" target="https://instances.social/">https://instances.social/</ref> was used and data collection was done on instances where data was publicly accessible, had at least 1,000 users, and contained posts including links to a rated news domain.

text.text: For Bluesky, the platform public API was employed to identify posts that linked to the rated domains.

For Telegram, from a database of 120,979 channels (25), 8,599 channels were randomly selected that had at least one post linking to a rated domain, and then the API was used to collect all posts and associated reaction data.
We also collected messages only from public channels, using a sample of channels identified in prior work (25), via the official Telegram API.
text.formatted: We also collected messages only from public channels, using a sample of channels identified in prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref>, via the official Telegram API.

text.text: Public channels are openly discoverable and readable by any Telegram user without invitation or approval; we did not collect data from private groups, invite-only channels, or chats.

News quality was assessed using a "wisdom of experts" approach that aggregates ratings from professional fact-checkers, journalists, and academics (domain list from Lin et al., 2023); each domain receives a normalized score between 0 and 1, where 0 is the lowest score given to any of the domains and 1 is the highest score given to any of the domains.
Thus, a higher score on the scale indicated high quality news and a lower score indicated low quality news (e.g., more likely source of misinformation).
All primary posts (not reshares or replies) were collected that contain a news domain shared by all types of users (e.g., regular users or organization accounts).
Political lean was estimated using GPT-4o by analyzing the lean of the news domain shared in the post, validated against established methods for measuring political orientation on social media (24).
text.formatted: Political lean was estimated using GPT-4o by analyzing the lean of the news domain shared in the post, validated against established methods for measuring political orientation on social media <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref>.

text.text: GPT-4o was asked to "Rate the domain DOMAIN on a scale of -5 (favors Democrats or liberals extremely) to 5 (favors Republicans or conservatives extremely).
If you are unsure, don't have enough information, or lack specific insights, please provide an educated or best guess.
Do not explain your response or limitations as a language model.
Provide a single number response.".

That is, if Fox News was the domain shared in the post, that post was determined to be right-leaning, if New York Times was the domain shared in the post, that post was determined to be left-leaning, etc.
The news headlines were retrieved for all URLs shared across platforms using the online service Diffbot.com.
For X and Mastodon, where the number of shared URLs was exceptionally large, quota sampling was applied based on news quality to preserve the original distribution.
We binned news quality rating by .2 then randomly sampled proportionally to the number of posts in each bin.
For X, we sampled 50% of posts and for Mastodon we sampled 10% of the posts.
To measure language toxicity we used Detoxify (https://github.com/unitaryai/detoxify) which is a validated model against Google Jigsaw's Perspective API (https://perspectiveapi.com/).
text.formatted: To measure language toxicity we used Detoxify (<ref type="url" target="https://github.com/unitaryai/detoxify">https://github.com/unitaryai/detoxify</ref>) which is a validated model against Google Jigsaw's Perspective API (<ref type="url" target="https://perspectiveapi.com/">https://perspectiveapi.com/</ref>).

text.text: To measure confidence, we used the Certainty Lexicon (13), a validated computational linguistic tool designed to quantify the level of confidence in text.
Each text is scored (from0 = "Very uncertain" to9 = "Very certain") using a comprehensive list of 3,485 words and phrases (e.g., "sorta" vs. "without doubt").

Compared to other text analysis tools, the Certainty Lexicon shows stronger correspondence with ground truth and more stable validity across text lengths, including social-media posts (see Figure SI1 and SI2 for distribution of linguistic confidence across platforms).
text.formatted: Compared to other text analysis tools, the Certainty Lexicon shows stronger correspondence with ground truth and more stable validity across text lengths, including social-media posts (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">SI1</ref> and SI2 for distribution of linguistic confidence across platforms).

text.text: Following prior work (24), we calculated engagement, defined as the sum of likes and reshares (except on Telegram, where only likes were available) (see Table SI1 for a summary).
text.formatted: Following prior work (24), we calculated engagement, defined as the sum of likes and reshares (except on Telegram, where only likes were available) (see Table <ref type="table">SI1</ref> for a summary).

text.text: We also validated the measure of linguistic confidence using human judgments of the social media posts (details in SI).
To measure emotionality, valence, and word count we used Evaluative Lexicon (32) (33).
text.formatted: To measure emotionality, valence, and word count we used Evaluative Lexicon <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(32)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(33)</ref>.

text.text: There was a total of 4,309,213 posts across 8,798 news domains for analysis.
We log transformed (log₁₀-transformed after adding 1 to account for zeros) engagement due to skew of the distribution and also used count regressions models for robustness check.
We also did a 100-tile transformation of toxicity due to the highly skewed nature of its distribution.

We used linear regressions with robust standard errors clustered by user (or by Telegram channel), and included models with user fixed effects to account for all individual-level variation in baseline engagement received.
All variables in the regression models are z-scored.

To assess whether the association between information quality and linguistic confidence is stable over time, we estimated a single linear regression predicting information quality from linguistic confidence interacted with day-of-study indicators, controlling for platform (i.e., using platform fixed effects), with standard errors clustered by user and variables z-scored on the pooled sample.
The base association was negative on all 31 days (only for one day the association was positive when we controlled for other language features) of the study period (Fig. SI8).

We further examined whether the association holds across topics.

We classified posts into four topical categories (science, politics, health, and economy) using TwHIN-BERT-large, a multilingual transformer model developed for social-media text and pretrained on approximately seven billion tweets in more than 100 languages (31).
text.formatted: We classified posts into four topical categories (science, politics, health, and economy) using TwHIN-BERT-large, a multilingual transformer model developed for social-media text and pretrained on approximately seven billion tweets in more than 100 languages <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(31)</ref>.

text.text: For each post, the classifier produces a probability for each topic, and a topic label is assigned when that probability exceeds its class-specific threshold.
Because posts can carry multiple labels, each topic-specific slope is estimated among posts assigned that label.
We then estimated a single regression predicting information quality from linguistic confidence interacted with topic indicators, controlling for platform, with standard errors clustered by user.

The association between linguistic confidence and information quality was significantly negative within every topic: Without controls: Politics, b = -0.026, SE = 0.003, t = -8.45, p < 0.001; Economy, b = -0.018, SE = 0.004, t = -4.01, p < 0.001; Health, b = -0.067, SE = 0.005, t = -13.32, p < 0.001; Science, b = -0.040, SE = 0.007, t = -5.98, p < 0.001; posts with None of these topics, b = -0.025, SE = 0.002, t = -14.37, p < 0.001.

text.text: Taken together, these results establish a robust and generalizable negative association between linguistic confidence and news quality, across platforms, textual sources, levels of analysis, time, and topical domains.

text.text: Cross-platform confidence-quality relationship -Tests whether linguistic confidence predicts the quality of news sources shared across platforms.
Greater linguistic confidence is associated with lower-quality news, and the relationship remains significant after controlling for political lean and other linguistic features.
Within-user analysis -Tests whether the relationship holds when comparing higher-versus lower-confidence posts from the same user.
The negative confidence-quality relationship persists within users, and remains significant after controlling for political lean and other linguistic features.
Post-level quality validation -Tests whether confidence predicts false or misleading information at the individual-post level rather than only outlet-level quality.
More confident posts are more likely to contain false or misleading information, including when accounting for user fixed effects.
Platform-level analysis -Tests whether platforms with greater average linguistic confidence also contain lower-quality shared news.
Platforms characterized by more confident language tend to have lower average news quality.
Headline and user-generated text -Tests whether the relationship appears in news headlines as well as users' own commentary.
The confidence-quality relationship appears in both headline language and user-generated content.
For headlines, the relationship remains significant after controlling for political lean and other linguistic features.
Engagement analysis -Tests whether more confident posts receive greater engagement from the same user's audience.

Greater linguistic confidence is associated with more engagement, including both likes and shares, and remains significant after controlling for political lean, news-domain fixed effects, and other linguistic and content features.
Analyses across Political Leanings -Tests whether the confidence-quality relationship persists across different parts of the political spectrum and whether its strength varies by political leaning.
The negative relationship is observed across left-, center-, and right-leaning news domains, but is significantly stronger among right-leaning news domains.
Analysis over time -Tests whether the confidence-quality relationship is consistent across the observation period.
The negative relationship is consistently observed across days.
Analysis across topics -Tests whether the relationship generalizes across science, politics, health, and economic news.
The negative confidence-quality relationship is observed across all four topical domains.

text.text: Although the Certainty Lexicon has been validated across contexts previously (Rocklage et al., 2023), we conducted a validation study to test whether Certainty Lexicon scores correspond to human judgments of certainty in the current context specifically.
text.formatted: Although the Certainty Lexicon has been validated across contexts previously <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Rocklage et al., 2023)</ref>, we conducted a validation study to test whether Certainty Lexicon scores correspond to human judgments of certainty in the current context specifically.

text.text: This study's methods, analyses, and criteria for success were preregistered (https://researchbox.org/10953%20(CODE:%20KFRAJN)
text.formatted: This study's methods, analyses, and criteria for success were preregistered (<ref type="url" target="https://researchbox.org/10953%20(CODE:%20KFRAJN)">https://researchbox.org/10953  (CODE: KFRAJN)</ref>

text.text: To provide a range of scores, the validation set consisted of a stratified random sample of 90 posts: 30 posts from each of low, medium, and high Certainty Lexicon score percentiles (bottom 10%, 45-55%, and top 10%, respectively).

To ensure representation across platforms, each certainty level included at least one post from each platform, with the remaining posts allocated in proportion to each platform's prevalence in the full dataset.
We aimed to recruit 200 participants, and a total of 198 participants provided complete data.
Each participant rated five randomly selected posts.
For each post, participants rated how much certainty or uncertainty it expressed (0 = very uncertain,9 = very certain).
The primary measure was the average human certainty rating for each post.
Consistent with our preregistered exclusion rule, participants who provided the same rating to all five posts they evaluated were excluded from the primary analysis.
Five participants met this criterion, leaving 193 participants.
The preregistered primary analysis calculated the correlation between Certainty Lexicon scores and average human certainty ratings across the 90 posts.
We also preregistered that the validation would be considered successful if this correlation was positive and statistically significant (two-sided p < .05).
text.formatted: We also preregistered that the validation would be considered successful if this correlation was positive and statistically significant (two-sided p < .05).

text.text: With 90 posts, the study had 80% power to detect a correlation of approximately r = .29 or larger.
As predicted, Certainty Lexicon scores were positively associated with average human certainty ratings (r = .50, 95% CI [.33, .64], p < .001) 1 .
text.formatted: As predicted, Certainty Lexicon scores were positively associated with average human certainty ratings (r = .50, 95% CI [.33, .64], p < .001) <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">1</ref> .

text.text: Thus, posts that received higher Certainty Lexicon scores were also perceived as expressing significantly greater certainty by human judges, meeting the preregistered criterion for successful validation.
The primary analyses measure linguistic confidence using the Certainty Lexicon.

To assess whether the confidence-quality relationship depends on this particular linguistic measure, we repeated the focal analyses using three conceptually related categories from LIWC: certitude, tentative, and all-or-none (Boyd, Ashokkumar, & Pennebaker, 2022).
text.formatted: To assess whether the confidence-quality relationship depends on this particular linguistic measure, we repeated the focal analyses using three conceptually related categories from LIWC: certitude, tentative, and all-or-none (Boyd, Ashokkumar, & Pennebaker, 2022).

text.text: Certitude and all-or-none measure forms of more certain language, whereas tentative captures uncertainty and should therefore show relationships in the opposite direction.

We otherwise followed the same analytic approach as in the primary analyses: all variables in the regression models were z-scored, standard errors were clustered by user, and, where applicable, platform-specific estimates were meta-analyzed across the eight platforms.
We first examined the relationship between these alternative measures and news quality.

Consistent with the primary results, across platforms posts containing greater certitude were associated with lower-quality news (b = -0.0172, SE = 0.0046, z = -3.75, p < .001), as were posts containing greater all-or-none language (b = -0.0217, SE = 0.0059, z = -3.70, p < .001).
text.formatted: Consistent with the primary results, across platforms posts containing greater certitude were associated with lower-quality news (b = -0.0172, SE = 0.0046, z = -3.75, p < .001), as were posts containing greater all-or-none language (b = -0.0217, SE = 0.0059, z = -3.70, p < .001).

text.text: As expected, the relationship was the opposite for tentative language: posts containing more tentative language were associated with higher-quality news (b = 0.0258, SE = 0.0087, z = 2.96, p = .003).

When controlling for political lean, the relationships remained significant for certitude (b = -0.0141, SE = 0.0039, z = -3.59, p < .001) and all-or-none language (b = -0.0217, SE = 0.0069, z = -3.16, p = .002).
text.formatted: When controlling for political lean, the relationships remained significant for certitude (b = -0.0141, SE = 0.0039, z = -3.59, p < .001) and all-or-none language (b = -0.0217, SE = 0.0069, z = -3.16, p = .002).

text.text: The relationship for tentative language was also significant in the cross-platform meta-analysis when controlling for political lean (b = 0.0179, SE = 0.0089, z = 2.01, p = .044).
Next, we aggregated data from all platforms and found the same pattern.

Greater certitude was associated with lower news quality (b = -0.0207, SE = 0.0012, t = -17.52, p < .001), as was greater all-or-none language (b = -0.0399, SE = 0.0022, t = -17.86, p < .001), whereas greater tentative language was associated with higher news quality (b = 0.0255, SE = 0.0015, t = 16.50, p < .001).
text.formatted: Greater certitude was associated with lower news quality (b = -0.0207, SE = 0.0012, t = -17.52, p < .001), as was greater all-or-none language (b = -0.0399, SE = 0.0022, t = -17.86, p < .001), whereas greater tentative language was associated with higher news quality (b = 0.0255, SE = 0.0015, t = 16.50, p < .001).

text.text: These relationships remained significant when controlling for political lean (certitude: b = -0.0205, SE = 0.0009, t = -21.74, p < .001; all-or-none: b = -0.0330, SE = 0.0015, t = -21.99, p < .001; tentative: b = 0.0094, SE = 0.0013, t = 7.49, p < .001).
text.formatted: These relationships remained significant when controlling for political lean (certitude: b = -0.0205, SE = 0.0009, t = -21.74, p < .001; all-or-none: b = -0.0330, SE = 0.0015, t = -21.99, p < .001; tentative: b = 0.0094, SE = 0.0013, t = 7.49, p < .001).

text.text: We further tested whether these relationships could be accounted for by other linguistic and content features.
Consistent with the primary analyses, we simultaneously controlled for political lean, emotionality, valence, language toxicity, and number of words.

The same pattern emerged: greater certitude (b = -0.0135, SE = 0.0013, t = -10.64, p < .001) and all-or-none language (b = -0.0213, SE = 0.0021, t = -9.97, p < .001) continued to predict lower news quality, whereas greater tentative language predicted higher news quality (b = 0.0196, SE = 0.0017, t = 11.45, p < .001).
text.formatted: The same pattern emerged: greater certitude (b = -0.0135, SE = 0.0013, t = -10.64, p < .001) and all-or-none language (b = -0.0213, SE = 0.0021, t = -9.97, p < .001) continued to predict lower news quality, whereas greater tentative language predicted higher news quality (b = 0.0196, SE = 0.0017, t = 11.45, p < .001).

text.text: Accounting for variation in user-level baseline news quality using user fixed effects showed a similar pattern.

The same individual, when using greater certitude, was more likely to link to lower-quality news (b = -0.0066, SE = 0.0004, t = -14.86, p < .001), as was the case when using greater all-or-none language (b = -0.0076, SE = 0.0006, t = -13.32, p < .001).
text.formatted: The same individual, when using greater certitude, was more likely to link to lower-quality news (b = -0.0066, SE = 0.0004, t = -14.86, p < .001), as was the case when using greater all-or-none language (b = -0.0076, SE = 0.0006, t = -13.32, p < .001).

text.text: Conversely, the same individual was more likely to link to higher-quality news when using more tentative language (b = 0.0025, SE = 0.0005, t = 5.35, p < .001).
text.formatted: Conversely, the same individual was more likely to link to higher-quality news when using more tentative language (b = 0.0025, SE = 0.0005, t = 5.35, p < .001).

text.text: Results were similar when controlling for political lean (certitude: b = -0.0064, SE = 0.0004, t = -15.28, p < .001; all-or-none: b = -0.0074, SE = 0.0005, t = -13.61, p < .001; tentative: b = 0.0018, SE = 0.0004, t = 4.08, p < .001).
text.formatted: Results were similar when controlling for political lean (certitude: b = -0.0064, SE = 0.0004, t = -15.28, p < .001; all-or-none: b = -0.0074, SE = 0.0005, t = -13.61, p < .001; tentative: b = 0.0018, SE = 0.0004, t = 4.08, p < .001).

text.text: Finally, we included user fixed effects while simultaneously controlling for political lean, emotionality, valence, language toxicity, and number of words.

Greater certitude continued to significantly predict lower news quality (b = -0.0069, SE = 0.0007, t = -9.73, p < .001), as did greater all-or-none language (b = -0.0103, SE = 0.0009, t = -11.14, p < .001).
text.formatted: Greater certitude continued to significantly predict lower news quality (b = -0.0069, SE = 0.0007, t = -9.73, p < .001), as did greater all-or-none language (b = -0.0103, SE = 0.0009, t = -11.14, p < .001).

text.text: Tentative language remained in the expected opposite direction, although the relationship was no longer significant in this most stringent specification (b = 0.0013, SE = 0.0008, t = 1.56, p = .119).
We additionally examined whether the relationship between linguistic confidence and engagement generalized to these LIWC measures.
As in the primary analyses, these models included user fixed effects so that we test whether the same user tends to receive more engagement when using more versus less confident language.

In the pooled analysis, greater all-or-none language predicted greater engagement (b = 0.0058, SE = 0.0007, t = 8.82, p < .001), while greater tentative language predicted less engagement (b = -0.0080, SE = 0.0005, t = -17.31, p < .001).
text.formatted: In the pooled analysis, greater all-or-none language predicted greater engagement (b = 0.0058, SE = 0.0007, t = 8.82, p < .001), while greater tentative language predicted less engagement (b = -0.0080, SE = 0.0005, t = -17.31, p < .001).

text.text: Certitude was positively but not significantly associated with engagement in this specification (b = 0.0005, SE = 0.0008, t = 0.68, p = .495).

Controlling for political lean produced virtually identical results (certitude: b = 0.0005, SE = 0.0008, t = 0.68, p = .495; tentative: b = -0.0080, SE = 0.0005, t = -17.33, p < .001; all-or-none: b = 0.0058, SE = 0.0007, t = 8.86, p < .001).
text.formatted: Controlling for political lean produced virtually identical results (certitude: b = 0.0005, SE = 0.0008, t = 0.68, p = .495; tentative: b = -0.0080, SE = 0.0005, t = -17.33, p < .001; all-or-none: b = 0.0058, SE = 0.0007, t = 8.86, p < .001).

text.text: The cross-platform meta-analysis showed a similar pattern.
Greater all-or-none language was significantly associated with greater engagement (b = 0.0061, SE = 0.0016, z = 3.72, p < .001).
text.formatted: Greater all-or-none language was significantly associated with greater engagement (b = 0.0061, SE = 0.0016, z = 3.72, p < .001).

text.text: Greater tentative language was significantly associated with less engagement (b = -0.0084, SE = 0.0029, z = -2.91, p = .004), whereas certitude was not associated with engagement (b = -0.0004, SE = 0.0009, z = -0.40, p = .689).

These results were similar when controlling for political lean (certitude: b = -0.0005, SE = 0.0009, z = -0.54, p = .586; tentative: b = -0.0084, SE = 0.0029, z = -2.89, p = .004; all-or-none: b = 0.0060, SE = 0.0016, z = 3.66, p < .001).

text.text: Finally, we examined the fuller engagement specification controlling for news quality, language toxicity, emotionality, valence, and number of words.

In these models, greater certitude significantly predicted greater engagement (b = 0.0016, SE = 0.0006, t = 2.65, p = .008), while greater tentative language significantly predicted less engagement (b = -0.0104, SE = 0.0007, t = -15.40, p < .001).

text.text: Greater all-or-none language remained positively and significantly associated with engagement (b = 0.0056, SE = 0.0007, t = 7.73, p < .001).

text.text: Taken together, the LIWC measures provide converging evidence for the relationship between linguistic confidence and information quality.

The confidence-quality relationship is particularly consistent: across all three LIWC measures, more certain and less tentative language is associated with lower-quality news, including after accounting for political lean and other linguistic features and, for certitude and all-or-none, in the most stringent within-user specification.
The engagement relationship also generalizes across multiple alternative measures, although the pattern is less uniform across specifications than the relationship with news quality.

In this pre-registered study, we validate the information quality scoring generated by two LLMs, GPT-4o and LLM Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite (without websearch), using two independent professional fact-checkers from Upwork.
Following prior work (30), we compare agreement between the human fact-checkers with average agreement between the LLM and each of the human fact-checkers.
text.formatted: Following prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(30)</ref>, we compare agreement between the human fact-checkers with average agreement between the LLM and each of the human fact-checkers.

text.text: Each fact-checker completed the task independently and was compensated through the platform.
The stimulus set consisted of 60 social media posts drawn from the corpus used in the main analyses.

Posts were selected on the basis of GPT-4o's classification, yielding three sets of 20 posts each: posts GPT-4o classified as false (mean LLM composite score = 1.00 on a 1-7 scale, where higher values indicate higher information quality), true (M = 6.88), and unsure (M = 4.12).

The posts originated from eight platforms (Telegram, n = 30; X, n = 11; Mastodon, n = 5; Bluesky, n = 4; Gab, n = 3; Truth Social, n = 3; LinkedIn, n = 2; Gettr, n = 2) and ranged from 58 to 1,945 characters in length.
The fact-checkers were not informed of the GPT-4o's ratings or of how the stimulus set was composed.
For each post, the fact-checkers and the LLMs answered the same questions, using the same response options and rating scales.

After providing informed consent, fact-checkers were told that they would see a series of short social media posts, one at a time, and were asked to read each post carefully, to answer a few questions about how true, accurate, and trustworthy they thought it was, and to judge each post on its own.
The 60 posts were then presented one at a time in an order randomized separately for each fact-checker.
Each post first appeared on its own page.
The three questions that followed were each presented on a separate page, with the text of the post repeated above each question so that it remained visible while the fact-checker responded.

The first question -on which we focus -measured the overall impression of the post's veracity ("What is your overall impression of the main claim in this post?"), with four response options: True, Misleading, False, and Not sure.
As this question is categorical, it allows for a straightforward assessment of agreement between raters.

Following prior work (30), we also asked various 7-point Likert measures about perceived bias ("Do you think this post is written in an unbiased way?") and perceived accuracy and credibility ("This post is objective," "This post describes something that actually happened," "This post is accurate," "This post is reliable," "This post is trustworthy," and "This post is true"), but we do not analyze those responses here.
text.formatted: Following prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(30)</ref>, we also asked various 7-point Likert measures about perceived bias ("Do you think this post is written in an unbiased way?") and perceived accuracy and credibility ("This post is objective," "This post describes something that actually happened," "This post is accurate," "This post is reliable," "This post is trustworthy," and "This post is true"), but we do not analyze those responses here.

text.text: Responses to all questions were required, so each fact-checker provided a complete set of ratings for all 60 posts.
The two fact-checkers gave the same overall assessment for 45 of the 60 posts (75.0%).
Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite agreed with Fact-checker 1 on 76.7% of posts and with Fact-checker 2 on 85% of posts, yielding an average agreement with fact-checkers of 80.8%.
GPT-4o mini agreed with Fact-checker 1 on 63.3% of posts and with Fact-checker 2 on 66.7% of posts, yielding an average agreement with fact-checkers of 65%.
Thus, consistent with prior work (30), Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite showed quite good agreement with the fact-checkers.
This validates our use of Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite to fact-check the posts in our dataset.
